scenes.title: Patroclus Pleads with Achilles
scenes.summary: While the fight goes on around the ship, Patroclus comes to Achilles weeping like a spring of dark water. Achilles asks why he cries like a little girl tugging at her mother's dress: has he news from Phthia, or is he grieving for the Argives who die at the ships for their own transgression? Patroclus tells him that the best of the Achaeans lie wounded, calls him pitiless, born not of Peleus and Thetis but of the gray sea and the sheer rocks, and asks, as Nestor advised, to be sent out in Achilles' armor at the head of the Myrmidons, so that the Trojans may take him for Achilles. The narrator calls him a fool: he is begging for his own death. Achilles answers that no prophecy holds him back, only his grief at being robbed of his prize like a dishonored vagrant; but let the past be past. Patroclus may put on his armor and lead the Myrmidons, but he must drive the Trojans from the ships and come back, and not fight on toward Troy without him, or a god may meet him. Achilles wishes that every Trojan and Argive might die, and they two alone loose the sacred veil of Troy.

scenes.title: Fire on the Ships
scenes.summary: Ajax, worn out by the missiles, his helmet ringing and his shoulder tired from the shield, can no longer hold his ground. The narrator calls on the Muses to tell how fire first fell on the ships. Hector strikes Ajax's spear behind the point with his great sword and shears off the head; Ajax, left holding the docked shaft, recognizes the work of the gods, that Zeus is cutting short his plans and wills victory for the Trojans, and draws back. The Trojans throw fire on the ship, and the flame pours over it at once.

scenes.title: The Arming of Patroclus
scenes.summary: Achilles strikes his thighs and tells Patroclus to arm quickly, while he gathers the army. Patroclus puts on the armor of Achilles and takes two spears, but not the Pelian ash, which Chiron cut on Pelion for Peleus and which Achilles alone could wield. Automedon yokes the immortal horses Xanthus and Balius, foaled by the Harpy Podarge to the West Wind, with the mortal trace horse Pedasus, taken from the city of Eetion. Achilles arms the Myrmidons, who rush out like wolves that have eaten a stag and go to lap the dark water of a spring, their bellies swollen with blood.

scenes.title: The Leaders of the Myrmidons
scenes.summary: Achilles brought fifty ships to Troy, fifty men in each, under five leaders: Menesthius, son of the river Spercheius and of Peleus' daughter Polydora, though by name the son of Borus; Eudorus, whom Polymele bore to Hermes after he saw her dancing in the chorus of Artemis, and whom her father Phylas reared when Echecles son of Actor married her; Peisander son of Maemalus, the best spearman after Patroclus; the old horseman Phoenix; and Alcimedon son of Laerces. Achilles reminds the Myrmidons how they threatened the Trojans all through his wrath and blamed him for keeping them by the ships: now the great work of battle they longed for is here. Their ranks close like the stones of a wall, shield on shield and helmet on helmet, and Patroclus and Automedon arm in front of them all.

scenes.title: Achilles' Prayer
scenes.summary: Achilles takes from the chest that Thetis gave him a cup that no one else drank from, cleans it with sulfur and water, pours wine and prays to Zeus of Dodona, the Pelasgian, around whom dwell the Selli, his interpreters, with unwashed feet, who sleep on the ground. As Zeus once heard his prayer and humbled the Achaeans, let him now give glory to Patroclus, and when he has driven the battle from the ships, bring him back safe with his armor and companions. Zeus grants the one and refuses the other. Achilles puts the cup away and stands in front of his hut to watch the battle.

scenes.title: The Myrmidons Drive the Trojans from the Ships
scenes.summary: The Myrmidons pour out like wasps by the wayside that boys have provoked, and Patroclus calls on them to win honor for Achilles and let Agamemnon see his blindness. His first spear kills Pyraechmes, the leader of the Paeonians, beside the stern of Protesilaus' ship; the Paeonians flee, Patroclus puts out the fire, and the half-burned ship is left. The Danaans breathe again, as when Zeus moves a thick cloud from a mountain peak and the boundless upper air breaks open, but the war has no respite, for the Trojans still resist.

scenes.title: Man Killed Man
scenes.summary: The leaders each kill a man: Patroclus Areilycus, Menelaus Thoas, Meges Amphiclus, Antilochus Atymnius, and Thrasymedes kills Atymnius' brother Maris as he stands over the body (they were sons of Amisodarus, who reared the Chimaera); Ajax son of Oileus takes Cleobulus alive and kills him with his sword; Peneleos and Lycon miss each other with their spears and close with swords, and Peneleos' sword sinks into Lycon's neck until only the skin holds the head; Meriones kills Acamas and Idomeneus Erymas. The Danaans fall on the Trojans like wolves on lambs and kids scattered on the mountains, and the Trojans forget their courage.

scenes.title: The Rout to the Ditch
scenes.summary: Ajax keeps trying to hit Hector, who knows that victory has turned but shelters under his shield and stands his ground to save his companions. The Trojans pour back toward the ditch in confusion; Hector's horses carry him over it, leaving the army behind, and many chariots break their poles in the ditch. The Trojan horses run groaning like the torrents of an autumn storm sent by Zeus in anger at men who give crooked judgments. Patroclus cuts off the foremost battalions and pens them between the ships, the river and the wall: he kills Pronous, drags Thestor son of Enops from his chariot on his spear like a fisherman landing a fish, splits Erylaus' head with a stone, and brings down nine more.

scenes.title: The Grief of Zeus
scenes.summary: Sarpedon rebukes the fleeing Lycians and leaps from his chariot to meet Patroclus, and the two rush at each other like vultures screaming on a high rock. Zeus, in pity, tells Hera that it is fated for Patroclus to kill Sarpedon, dearest of men, and that his heart is divided: should he snatch his son alive from the battle and set him down in Lycia? Hera warns that the other gods will not approve, and that others will want to save their sons too; let him die, and then send Death and sweet Sleep to carry him home, where his kinsmen will bury him with a mound and a pillar. Zeus agrees, and sheds drops of blood on the earth in honor of his son.

scenes.title: The Death of Sarpedon
scenes.summary: Patroclus kills Thrasymelus, Sarpedon's attendant. Sarpedon misses and kills the trace horse Pedasus, which falls screaming and tangles the team until Automedon cuts it loose. Sarpedon misses again, and Patroclus' spear strikes him where the midriff encloses the heart. He falls like an oak, a poplar or a tall pine felled for ship timber, and lies roaring before his chariot like a bull killed by a lion. Dying, he calls on Glaucus to rouse the Lycian leaders and fight for his body, for he will be a reproach to Glaucus forever if the Achaeans strip his armor. Death covers him, and Patroclus, his heel on his chest, draws out the spear, and with it the midriff and his soul.

scenes.title: Glaucus Rallies the Trojans
scenes.summary: Glaucus, still in pain from Teucer's arrow, prays to Apollo, who stops the pain, stanches the blood and fills him with might. He rouses the Lycian leaders and goes to Polydamas, Agenor, Aeneas and Hector, and rebukes Hector for forgetting his allies: Sarpedon, who guarded Lycia with his justice and his strength, has been killed by the spear of Patroclus, and the Myrmidons will strip and dishonor him. Grief seizes the Trojans, for Sarpedon was a bulwark of their city, though a stranger, and Hector leads them on. Patroclus rouses the two Ajaxes: the man who first leapt inside the Achaean wall lies dead; let them strip and dishonor him. The armies close around the body, and Zeus stretches deadly night over the battle.

scenes.title: The Fight for Sarpedon
scenes.summary: Hector kills the Myrmidon Epeigeus with a stone; once lord of Budeum, he had killed his cousin and fled as a suppliant to Peleus and Thetis. Patroclus darts through the front ranks like a hawk among jackdaws and starlings and kills Sthenelaus with a stone; Glaucus kills Bathycles, the wealthiest of the Myrmidons, and Meriones Laogonus, whose father Onetor was the priest of Idaean Zeus. Aeneas throws at Meriones and misses, and taunts him as a dancer; Meriones retorts, and Patroclus rebukes him: the outcome of war lies in the hands, and that of words in council.

scenes.title: Sleep and Death Carry Sarpedon Home
scenes.summary: The din of the fighting rises like that of woodcutters in the mountains, and men swarm around the body, covered with missiles, blood and dust, like flies around brimming milk pails in spring. Zeus ponders whether Hector should kill Patroclus there, and decides that Patroclus will first drive the Trojans back to the city. He puts a craven spirit in Hector, who flees, knowing the sacred scales of Zeus, and the Lycians flee from their dead king. The Achaeans strip Sarpedon's armor. Zeus tells Apollo to carry the body out of range, wash it in the river, anoint it with ambrosia, clothe it in immortal garments and send it with the twins Sleep and Death to Lycia; Apollo does all this.

scenes.title: Patroclus at the Wall of Troy
scenes.summary: Patroclus, blinded, the fool, pursues the Trojans; had he kept Achilles' word he would have escaped black death, but the mind of Zeus is stronger than men's. He kills Adrastus, Autonous, Echeclus, Perimus, Epistor, Melanippus, Elasus, Mulius and Pylartes. The Achaeans would have taken Troy, but Apollo stood on the tower: three times Patroclus climbs onto an angle of the wall and three times Apollo thrusts him back, and the fourth time warns him that the city is fated to fall neither to his spear nor to that of Achilles. Patroclus gives ground. At the Scaean gates Hector is wondering whether to fight on or call the army inside the wall, when Apollo, in the likeness of his uncle Asius son of Dymas, rebukes him and sends him against Patroclus.

scenes.title: The Death of Cebriones
scenes.summary: Hector drives at Patroclus, and Apollo throws the Argives into confusion. Patroclus leaps down and hits Hector's charioteer Cebriones, a bastard son of Priam, on the forehead with a jagged stone; his eyes fall in the dust and he plunges from the chariot like a diver, and Patroclus mocks him: what a nimble man, and how easily he dives; if he were at sea he would feed many, diving for oysters. Patroclus and Hector fight over the body like two lions over a slain deer, Hector holding the head and Patroclus a foot, while the rest clash around them like the East Wind and the South Wind in a forest. Cebriones lies in the whirling dust, great over a great space, forgetful of his horsemanship.

scenes.title: The Death of Patroclus
scenes.summary: As the sun moves on toward the time for unyoking oxen, the Achaeans prevail beyond their portion and strip Cebriones. Three times Patroclus charges and three times kills nine men; the fourth time Apollo meets him, hidden in mist, and strikes his back with the flat of his hand. His helmet rolls in the dust, his spear is shattered, his shield falls and Apollo loosens his corselet; blind folly seizes him and he stands dazed. Euphorbus, son of Panthous, wounds him in the back and runs off, and as Patroclus draws back among his companions Hector stabs him in the lower flank. Hector boasts over him, and Patroclus, dying, answers that Zeus and Apollo gave Hector the victory: fate and the son of Leto killed him, and of men Euphorbus, and Hector is only the third; death stands close beside Hector too, at the hands of Achilles. His soul flies to Hades, lamenting its fate, leaving manhood and youth. Hector answers the dead man, pulls out his spear, and chases Automedon, whom the immortal horses carry away.

days.label: Day 26
days.note: The third day of battle continues (11.1 to 18.242). The sun stands at the middle of the sky while the armies fight over Cebriones and moves on toward the time for unyoking oxen as Patroclus makes his last charge (16.777–780); Book 16 ends with Hector chasing Automedon.
